editorial.headline: Retail Clothing, Nationally Open but Off-Limits for Foreign Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers broad retail clothing sales across every business scale, with full national foreign ownership available but PMA registration blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
Retail clothing is the business of selling garments made from textiles, leather or artificial leather. Its scope runs from shirts, trousers, suits, coats and jackets to pyjamas, kebaya, blouses, skirts, house dresses, underwear, bras, gowns, baby clothes, dancewear, traditional dress, mukena and robes. It also includes general sportswear that has not been designed for one particular sport. This is deliberately a broad apparel-retail activity: the defining question is the retail sale of clothing within that stated range.

The activity is open to businesses at the Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. Nationally, its PMA status is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That makes the national position unusually direct: foreign investment can hold the full permitted stake in a business registered for this activity. The record attributes that national position to Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021.

Bali is where the picture changes decisively. In Bali today, a foreigner cannot register this activity as a PMA. The Bali classification is blocked on risk-class grounds, because at the Large scale its OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope. Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities from PMA registration. The result is not a reduced foreign-ownership percentage or a conditional local partnership route; it is a registration block for PMA on the island.

For a founder, the important discipline is to keep the two positions separate. National openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remain the national framework for this retail-clothing activity. They do not override the Bali moratorium. A business may fit the activity’s broad clothing scope and be eligible across all four listed scales, yet still be unable to make a PMA registration for it in Bali under the current risk-based provincial restriction. The practical reading is therefore clear: the activity is nationally open to foreign investment, but presently unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
